terms.definition: A hall whose roof is held up by rows of columns. The word is Greek for “resting on pillars”. In Egyptian temples it usually stands between the open court and the inner rooms. In the temple’s model of creation it stood for the papyrus marsh at the edge of the [[primeval-mound]].

A monumental temple gateway made of two massive towers with a doorway between them. Karnak’s pylons are numbered in the order a modern visitor meets them, not the order they were built. Its outline echoes the hieroglyph [[akhet]], “horizon”: the sun between two hills.

citations.locator: Egyptian architecture: pylon and the akhet hieroglyph

terms.definition: The wide, higher passage down the middle of the Hall, lined by the twelve tallest columns. It carried the temple’s main west–east route.
A raised band of wall with window openings, built where a higher roof meets a lower one. In the Hall, huge stone window grilles above the central aisle were the main source of light.
A stone beam laid across the tops of columns. Roof slabs rested on the architraves. In the Hall they also carry long dedication texts.
Small, standard-sized sandstone blocks used in the buildings of Akhenaten. After his reign they were dismantled and reused as fill, including in the foundations of the Hall.
One horizontal row of scenes on a wall. Most walls in the Hall have four or five registers, stacked one above the other, each scene in its own frame.
Carving in which the background is cut away so the figures and signs stand out from the wall. It is slow, careful work. All of Sety I’s carving inside the Hall is in raised relief.

Carving in which the outlines are cut down into the wall, so the figures sit below the original surface. It is quicker to make and throws strong shadows. Ramesses II switched to it early in his reign.
The oval ring, closed by a bar, that encloses a king’s name. Each king had two names written in cartouches: a throne name and a birth name.
The name a king took when he came to the throne, written in a cartouche. Sety I’s was Menmaatre; Ramesses II’s final form was Usermaatre-setepenre.
The king’s personal name, also written in a cartouche, often with an extra phrase such as “beloved of Amun”: for example Ramesses-meramun.
The hieroglyph for “life”: a loop above a crossbar and a stem. Gods hold it and offer it to kings; in the Hall, a king holding one is being shown as divine.

citations.locator: The ankh as a sign of divinity

terms.definition: Truth, justice and right order, and the goddess who stands for them, shown seated with an ostrich feather on her head. Kings offered Maat to the gods, and her figure appears in many royal names.
God of the dead and of renewal. A king who died was believed to become one with Osiris, so texts call a dead king “Osiris King …”.

A model boat carried on poles by priests, with a shrine holding the god’s statue. Each god had one: Amun’s has ram heads at both ends, Mut’s has a woman’s head, Khonsu’s a falcon’s head with a moon disk.
A spouted jar used for pouring water in purification rites.

citations.locator: Plate 48, p. 98: four nemset jars of water

terms.definition: The divine family worshipped at Karnak: Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu.
The dark, endless water that existed before anything else, in Egyptian belief: an ocean of nothingness. The world rose out of it.
A creator god, a form of the sun god. In the creation story behind temple design he floated asleep in [[nun]], woke, raised the first land and made everything else.
The first dry land, which rose out of [[nun]] at the very first moment of creation. The creator stood on it to make the world. A temple’s innermost sanctuary stood for this mound.
God of the air. With [[tefnut]], the first child of [[atum]]. Father of [[geb]] and [[nut]].
Goddess of moisture. With [[shu]], the first child of [[atum]]. Mother of [[geb]] and [[nut]].
God of the earth, child of [[shu]] and [[tefnut]].
Goddess of the sky, child of [[shu]] and [[tefnut]].

The innermost room of a temple, where the god’s statue stood. Small, nearly dark, with the highest floor and the lowest ceiling in the building. It stood for the [[primeval-mound]]. Only the king and a few priests went in.
The statue of the god kept in the sanctuary, the focus of the temple’s daily rituals. In the temple’s model of creation, a single small light shaft fell on it in the dark.
Egyptian for “horizon”. The hieroglyph shows the sun between two hills, the place where it rises and sets. The two towers of a [[pylon]] echo this sign.

citations.locator: Egyptian architecture: pylon and the akhet hieroglyph

terms.definition: A tall, four-sided stone shaft with a small pyramid at the top, cut from a single block, usually of red granite from Aswan. Kings set them up in pairs in front of temple gateways.

citations.locator: Thutmose I; Hatshepsut; Thutmose III (obelisk pairs)
